configs.name: rules-baseline
configs.description: Rule-based planner, default limits (3 rounds, 24 tool calls, stop at 0.75)

configs.name: rules-single-round
configs.description: Triage round only: no targeted follow-up evidence

configs.name: rules-eager-stop
configs.description: Stops as soon as the leading hypothesis reaches 0.55

configs.name: rules-no-knowledge
configs.description: Ablation: knowledge base / incident history tools unavailable

configs.name: llm-planner
configs.description: LLM intake + planning (default prompt), rubric confidence

configs.name: llm-planner-hypothesis-first
configs.description: LLM planning with a prompt that asks for one disconfirming check per hypothesis

judge.rationale: The ground truth root cause is a dependency failure in the payments-provider starting at 7 min, while the report incorrectly identifies Redis as the primary root cause (which was an independent issue starting at 9 min). Although the report mentions the payments provider as an alternative, it attributes the main incident to Redis and recommends actions primarily for Redis, thus missing the correct primary root cause.

The recommended action to escalate to the infrastructure team aligns with the expected manual network remediation. The explanation cites specific p95 latencies and affected services correctly.

rows.summary: Most probable cause: Slow queries on PostgreSQL (low confidence, 0.48).

judge.rationale: The investigation correctly identifies database degradation in postgres as the domain, but stops at the symptom ('slow queries') rather than identifying the root cause (dropped index by manual DBA change). Therefore, per the prompt instructions, the verdict must be 'partially_correct'. The explanation is coherent and uses supporting metrics like pool saturation, and the recommendation to investigate postgres provides moderate actionability.

rows.summary: Most probable cause: The third-party payments provider is failing (medium confidence, 0.65).

judge.rationale: The automated investigation correctly identified the root cause as a failure of the third-party payments-provider, matching the ground truth. The explanation cites solid supporting metrics and logs showing error ratios and latency. The actions recommended (contacting the provider, failover) are practical and actionable for the on-call engineer.
